issues.legal_issue: A prosecution’s failure to examine a cited witness who was never tendered as evidence does not constitute rejection of evidence under section 167 of the Indian Evidence Act.
material_facts: The prosecution cited a witness who refused to testify, claiming constitutional protection.
The prosecution then dropped the witness and did not tender him as a witness.
The defence did not seek to call the witness, and the court did not know what his testimony would have been.
issues.conclusion: Section 167 did not assist the appellants because the witness’s evidence had not been rejected within the meaning of that section.
issues.legal_principle: Section 167 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, was inapplicable because the prosecution did not tender the witness and his evidence was not rejected; the Court did not decide whether the witness was entitled to claim protection under Article 20 of the Constitution.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_nonexaminati: The accused brought a criminal appeal challenging the failure to examine a witness.
predicates.prosecution_did_not_tender_witness: The prosecution did not present the cited witness to give evidence.
predicates.defence_did_not_seek_witness: The accused did not seek to call the witness for the defence.

issues.definition: When an accused challenges a conviction in a criminal appeal, evidence is not treated as rejected if the prosecution never tendered the witness and the defence did not seek to call that witness.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution is not required to call a witness who is not essential to unfolding its case, and failure to call such a witness does not by itself vitiate the trial.
material_facts: The charged offences concerned the assault on a person and his abduction.
The witness arrived only after the assault and abduction had occurred and could not give evidence about those charged events.
The witness’s later involvement in a separate incident was not necessary to prove the charged offences.
The prosecution did not call him, and the accused did not seek to produce him as a defence witness.
issues.conclusion: The witness was not material to the prosecution’s case, the prosecution was not bound to call him, and the trial was not vitiated by his absence.
issues.legal_principle: Under the test stated in Stephen Seneviratne v. The King, A.I.R. 1936 P.C. 289, a material witness for this purpose is one essential to unfolding the narrative on which the prosecution is based, not merely one who might support the defence. As recognized in Habeeb Mohammad v. The State of Hyderabad, [1954] S.C.R. 475, deliberately or unfairly withholding a material witness may cast serious doubt on the propriety of the trial and expose the resulting conviction to challenge. The prosecution must call material witnesses to prove its own case, but need not call witnesses merely to establish the defence or duplicate evidence.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction_f: The accused brought a criminal appeal arguing that the conviction was affected by the prosecution’s failure to call a witness.
predicates.witness_arrived_after_charged_events: The witness came onto the scene only after the events underlying the charged offences had occurred.
predicates.witness_could_not_testify_to_charged_eve: The witness was not in a position to give evidence about the facts on which the prosecution relied to prove the charged offences.

issues.definition: A conviction is not invalidated for failure to call a witness in a criminal appeal when that witness arrived after the charged events and could not testify to them.

issues.legal_issue: A higher sentence may be justified by an offender’s role in directing an attack even when the evidence does not establish that the offender caused a particular grievous injury.
material_facts: The evidence did not establish that the appellant personally caused the grievous injury relied on in the sentencing argument.
The appellant directed the attacking party to pursue the victim, after which serious injuries were inflicted.
The appeal challenged the sentence, and the Court considered the appellant’s role in the attack.
issues.conclusion: The higher sentence was justified by the appellant’s role in directing the attack, notwithstanding the lack of evidence that he caused the particular grievous injury.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the sentence by reference to the appellant’s conduct in directing the attack and the serious injuries that followed; it relied on no cited provision or earlier case for this sentencing conclusion.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_sentence and specific_grievous_injury_attribution_unproved and offender_directed_attack and serious_injuries_followed_attack

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_sentence: The offender brought a criminal appeal challenging the sentence imposed for the offence.
predicates.specific_grievous_injury_attribution_unp: The evidence did not establish that the offender personally caused the particular grievous injury relied on in challenging the sentence.
predicates.offender_directed_attack: The offender directed or urged others to attack the victim.
predicates.serious_injuries_followed_attack: Serious injuries were inflicted on the victim after the offender directed the attack.

issues.definition: A higher sentence is justified by an offender’s role in directing an attack when the offender’s personal causation of a particular grievous injury is unproved but serious injuries followed the attack.
